newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: FOCUS-LITHUANIAN T-BILL MARKET SEEN AS CONFIDENCE TEST.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LITHUANIAN T-BILL MARKET SEEN AS CONFIDENCE TEST.

text.p: The response to Lithuania's launch of long-term Treasury bills will be a key test of the market's confidence in the government's plans to gradually scrap the country's currency board, analysts say.

The country's finance ministry plans to diversify its debt market and introduce two-year T-bills in September and paper with a five-year maturity early next year. Maturities currently run from one month to one year.
The move to longer maturities coincides with the central bank's transition to a more active monetary policy and the elimination of of the currency board.

Under the system, adopted in 1994 with the blessing of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the country's central bank guarantees that it will have one dollar in reserve for every four litas in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
The system has kept the currency rigidly stable, a fact not lost on investors, who have found Lithuania's domestic debt market attractive.
Yields have been falling recently and have stabilised in the nine to ten percent range.
But the longer maturities will be the first real test of the market's take on the government's currency plans.

"We are not expecting that at the first auction there would be a very good price for the issue...it is just to open the way for the next issue," Arvydas Kregzde, director of the central bank's market operations department, told Reuters.

After sweeping into power in last autumn's parlaimentary elections, Lithuania's centre-right government had trouble convincing currency and debt markets that the litas would stay stable during the return to a central bank system.
To calm fears, the government and central bank have stressed the incremental nature of their plans.
The dollar peg is not seen being changed before 1999. According to officials, the peg may at that point be "revised" to include EU currencies alongside the dollar.
The central bank says that confidence in its plans can be seen in the growing popularity of longer-term T-bills.
"At first it was mostly one-month T-bills, and now the most popular are the six-month T-bills," Kregzde said.
But as the Czech crown takes a pounding, not all investors are convinced that the litas can stand without the support of the currency board.
"It (long-term Lithuanian T-bills) is certainly not a safe investment for an investor like me," said Kristjan Hanni, head of asset management at Estonia's Hoiupank.
Others say they have been reassured by the central bank and are positive about Lithuania's long-term prospects.
"We have heard from the central bank that the exit from the currency board will be handled in the right way," said Henri Malvet, assistant vice president of Finland's Merita Bank Ltd.

"Of course there is a risk, but if there is a higher risk on T-bills, there is also a higher reward," said Piotr Borovski, director of Poland's Kredyt Bank S.A. "I think investors can accept the risks in Lithuania."
According to a key Western observer, the switch from the currency board may actually leave many aspects of monetary policy unchanged.
"I would stress continuity rather than change in the system," said Lithuania's IMF Resident Representative, Domenico Fanizza.
"Practically, they are going to maintain the same policies as they have now," Fanizza added.
